entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Arab Ba'ath Party (Hizb al-Ba'ath al-'Arabi — 'Arab Resurrection Party'), founded in Damascus in 1947 by Michel Aflaq and Salah al-Din al-Bitar, was the pan-Arab socialist party that governed Iraq (1968-2003) and Syria (1963-present) — its two branches conducting opposite paths from the same ideological origin, with Saddam Hussein's Iraq and Hafez al-Assad's Syria becoming bitter enemies despite sharing Ba'athist governance. The Ba'ath Party's influence on Middle Eastern authoritarianism, from Iraq's genocidal 1988 Anfal campaign against Kurds to Syria's 2011 brutal civil war suppression, defines 20th-century Arab nationalist state violence.

Michel Aflaq, a Greek Orthodox Christian Arab nationalist, and Salah al-Din al-Bitar founded the Arab Ba'ath Party with the slogan 'Unity, Freedom, Socialism' (Wahda, Hurriyya, Ishtirakiyya). The party's core ideology combined pan-Arab nationalism (all Arabs are one nation with a common language, history, and destiny) with secular socialism. Ba'ath came to power in Syria in 1963 and Iraq in 1968 through military coups.

In Iraq, Saddam Hussein dominated Ba'athist governance from 1969 (as party strongman) and became president in 1979. The 1988 Anfal campaign (using chemical weapons against Kurdish villages, killing 50,000-182,000 civilians) and the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq War (500,000-1 million dead) were the regime's most catastrophic actions. The 2003 US-led invasion and Paul Bremer's De-Ba'athification — dissolving the Iraqi military and banning Ba'ath Party members from public service — created the power vacuum that produced Al-Qaeda in Iraq and later ISIS.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Ba'ath Party's two branches — Saddam's Iraq and Assad's Syria — conducted the Arab world's most catastrophic 20th-century state violence; and De-Ba'athification's 2003 vacuum produced ISIS, making the party's dissolution as consequential as its rule.
